input_signals.name: OpaqueValueAccrualInstability
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1), RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(wcap, 1), dp), at), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness is only investable when the accounting is legible: firms with volatile, unstable accruals are informationally opaque, so their low multiples reflect justified uncertainty, while cheap firms with stable accrual behavior are genuinely mispriced.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the level of accruals with the second moment of accruals, a distinct information-risk mechanism rather than an earnings-overstatement mechanism, gated onto an EBITDA-based cheapness measure that is itself pre-accrual. If it outperforms Signal 1, the interaction is about accounting reliability rather than accrual direction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( ebitda, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 ), rank( neg( vol( ratio( sub( delta( wcap, 1 ), dp ), at ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ConjunctiveValueAccrualScreen
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(wcap, 1), dp), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness and accrual conservatism are complements, not substitutes: the value premium is earned only when a firm passes both screens, so the expected return is governed by the weaker of the two percentile scores rather than by their average.
input_signals.reasoning: Working in bounded industry-rank space removes the negative-book-equity perversity of the multiplicative gate, since a good accrual rank can no longer push a distressed firm further into the short leg. The MIN aggregation is a substantively different claim from the published additive value-plus-accruals composite: it predicts no premium for accrual-clean expensive firms or for accrual-heavy cheap firms, which a linear blend rewards partially.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( delta( wcap, 1 ), dp ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualRegimeReversalValue
input_signals.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(wcap, 1), dp), at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheap firms whose current accruals sit at the low end of their own five-year accrual history have already absorbed the reversal of past aggressive reporting; the market extrapolates the recent weak reported earnings, so the discount is stale and mean-reverts upward.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the flawed "purged equity" arithmetic entirely, so no depreciation add-back can inflate the valuation anchor: depreciation enters only inside a self-referenced time-series rank, where firm-level capital intensity is differenced away. The mechanism is a within-firm accrual regime state (reversal completed) interacted with cross-sectional cheapness, which is distinct from any accrual-level composite.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ts_rank( ratio( sub( delta( wcap, 1 ), dp ), at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: HardBookToMarket
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(ceq, SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc))), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
input_signals.hypothesis: Book equity composed of receivables, inventories and other soft operating working capital is far less reliable collateral for a value claim than equity composed of cash and long-lived assets; restating the value anchor on hard, non-accrual equity identifies cheapness that is not an artifact of accrual-inflated current assets.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not operating cash flow to price, because it uses the stock of net operating working capital rather than its change, so it cannot collapse to the documented CF/P anomaly and it prices the accumulated accrual balance that reversal risk actually lives on. Firms whose book equity is mostly working capital receive a sharply lower signal even at identical B/M, which is exactly the value-trap distinction the theme calls for.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( ceq, sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ) ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) )

input_signals.name: CashEbitdaToEnterpriseValue
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(ebitda, DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Operating profit that must be reinvested in receivables and inventories is not distributable to capital providers; measuring cheapness as working-capital-adjusted EBITDA per dollar of enterprise value identifies firms whose whole-capital-structure multiple is supported by cash-convertible profit rather than by working-capital-inflated accounting profit.
input_signals.reasoning: The enterprise-value denominator prices debt and net cash, making this a different valuation anchor from book-to-market and hence less collinear with HML, while the numerator subtracts the exact accrual component that makes EBITDA unreliable. It tests whether moving the interaction into an EV multiple recovers the FF5 alpha that equity-only value anchors failed to deliver.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( ebitda, delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), sub( add( dltt, dlc ), che ) ) )

input_signals.name: CheapnessWeightedAccrualQuality
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(wcap, 1), dp), at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accrual conservatism is priced only where the market has already assigned a low multiple, so the correct signal is accrual quality amplified by the firm's cheapness percentile: among expensive firms the accrual term is muted, among cheap firms it fully separates cash-backed value from accrual-supported value traps.
input_signals.reasoning: Unlike the symmetric z-score product, one leg is a bounded [0,1] cheapness weight and only the accrual leg is signed, so the long and short extremes are both drawn from cheap firms (clean versus dirty) instead of pooling cheap-clean with expensive-dirty. That construction also makes the spread approximately value-neutral, which directly targets the gen-1 failure in which static-value loadings caused FF5 to absorb or over-price the entire raw spread.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( neg( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( wcap, 1 ), dp ), at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CashFundedExpansionValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUB(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), at), RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: For a cheap firm the informative question is what its balance sheet grew into: cash accumulation means reported profits were collected, while growth concentrated in receivables and inventories means profits exist only on paper, so the cash-versus-soft-capital composition of expansion discriminates real from illusory cheapness.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the flawed price-driven "value news" leg — which was mechanically past return and thus a reversal bet — with a purely fundamental composition measure that contains no price change at all. Because the cheapness term enters as a bounded weight, the long-short spread again compares cheap firms with cheap firms, so the mechanism is testable without an embedded HML position.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( sub( ratio( delta( che, 1 ), at ), ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CurrentLiabilityStretchedValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(lct, 1), MA(sale, 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheap firms that expand payables and accrued liabilities faster than their normalized revenue are financing operations by stretching suppliers and deferring recognized costs, which simultaneously flatters operating cash flow and raises refinancing risk, so their low multiple reflects a deteriorating rather than a temporarily depressed business.
input_signals.reasoning: This tests the liability side of the accrual construct, a channel none of the archived signals touches, and normalizing by three-year average sales avoids the scale artifacts of asset deflation for firms with shrinking balance sheets. Because it explicitly predicts a negative slope within the cheap cohort, it also serves as the sign-symmetric counterpart to Signal 2: both should be strong if the trap mechanism is real, and their disagreement would localize whether asset-side or liability-side accruals drive the effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( ratio( delta( lct, 1 ), ma( sale, 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: WorstFlawPenalizedValue
input_signals.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MAX(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(wcap, 1), dp), at), 1)), IND_RANK(ABS(RATIO(aoloch, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accounting credibility is destroyed by whichever red flag is worst, not by their average: a cheap firm is a trap if either its working-capital accruals are large or its cash-flow reconciliation is dominated by unexplained other-accrual items, so cheapness should be penalized by the maximum of the two flaw percentiles.
input_signals.reasoning: The MAX operates on the accrual side rather than across themes, which is a different aggregation claim from the archived MIN screen: it lets two economically distinct accounting flaws substitute for each other as disqualifiers while keeping a single continuous value ladder. Winsorizing the accrual leg and using absolute opacity keeps both flaw measures sign-unambiguous and bounded, and comparing this to the archived single-flaw versions tells us whether accrual red flags are additive or worst-case in their pricing effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), max( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( wcap, 1 ), dp ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( abs( ratio( aoloch, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: WorkingCapitalTurnoverValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(sale, SUB(act, che))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accrual assets are only dangerous when they are unproductive: a cheap firm that turns each dollar of receivables and inventory into many dollars of revenue is converting accruals into realized sales quickly, while a cheap firm with slow working-capital turnover is warehousing claims that will be written down.
input_signals.reasoning: This introduces a new channel — the velocity of accrual assets rather than their level, change, or composition — while keeping the cheapness-weight structure that produced the archive's only positive alpha. Turnover is a strictly positive, well-scaled quantity with broad coverage, and industry z-scoring removes the large sector differences in normal operating-cycle length.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( ratio( sale, sub( act, che ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualNonArticulationValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ABS(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), NEG(ADD(recch, ADD(invch, apalch))))), at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: When the balance-sheet change in working capital does not reconcile with the working-capital items reported in the cash-flow statement, the gap reflects acquisitions, reclassifications, write-offs and other discretion that makes the accounting hard to audit; cheapness is credible when the two accrual measurements articulate and is a trap when they diverge.
input_signals.reasoning: The discriminating variable is neither the level nor the direction of accruals but the internal consistency of two independent measurements of the same accrual — a measurement-integrity channel the archive has never tested, and one that is zero for a clean, organically operating firm regardless of how large its accruals are. Winsorizing and asset-scaling the discrepancy keeps it bounded, and pairing it with the bounded cheapness weight retains the value-neutral spread structure, at the cost of the narrower coverage of the cash-flow-statement working-capital items.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( neg( winsor( ratio( abs( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), neg( add( recch, add( invch, apalch ) ) ) ) ), at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: TurnoverImprovementValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(sale, SUB(act, che)), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A cheap firm whose working-capital turnover is accelerating is liquidating accrual assets into realized sales and thereby validating its depressed multiple, whereas slowing turnover at a low multiple signals inventory and receivables accumulating faster than the business can convert them.
input_signals.reasoning: Paired with Signal 1 this decomposes the velocity channel into a structural level and a directional change, which is the key unresolved design question for the archive's best joint result. Unlike the earlier flagged change signals, no price term enters the change leg, so it cannot degenerate into a past-return reversal bet.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( delta( ratio( sale, sub( act, che ) ), 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: OperatingCycleInstabilityValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(VOL(RATIO(sale, SUB(act, che)), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness is credible when the operating cycle is predictable: a firm whose working-capital turnover swings erratically has accrual assets whose realizable value is unknowable to outsiders, so its discount reflects genuine information risk rather than mispricing.
input_signals.reasoning: This adds the second moment of the velocity channel, distinguishing "fast" from "reliable" conversion, and it revisits the instability idea that failed in gen 1 with an EBITDA-yield anchor and a Sloan-flow volatility measure — now applied to the operating-cycle variable that actually generates alpha. If stability dominates level, refinement should move toward predictability metrics; if not, the channel is purely about speed.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( neg( vol( ratio( sale, sub( act, che ) ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationConservatismValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(dp, MA(at, 3)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Long-lived asset accounting, not just working capital, determines whether cheapness is real: a firm that charges heavy depreciation relative to its normalized asset base is writing its assets down aggressively, so its book equity and reported earnings are understated and its low multiple overstates how expensive it truly is, while a cheap firm with unusually light depreciation is carrying stale asset values that will eventually be impaired.
input_signals.reasoning: This moves the accrual leg from the working-capital cycle — the only accrual channel the archive has explored — to the depreciation channel, which is the second large non-cash component of earnings and is entirely untested here, so the result is informative regardless of sign. Industry z-scoring strips out sector capital intensity so the surviving variation is within-industry accounting conservatism, and three-year average assets in the denominator avoids the mechanical spike that a shrinking asset base would create.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( dp, ma( at, 3 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: VelocityScreenedValue
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(sale, SUB(act, che)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness and operating-asset velocity are complements that must both be present: a firm qualifies as cash-verified value only if it is cheap *and* converts its receivables and inventories into revenue quickly, so expected return is governed by the weaker of the two percentile scores rather than by a soft product of a weight and a score.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates one specific design choice — hard weakest-link screening versus the soft rank-times-z-score weighting — on the only mechanism in the archive that is significant on both the cross-sectional and portfolio dimensions, and MIN-of-ranks was previously the structure that produced the archive's strongest FMB slope (4.36). Because both legs are bounded industry ranks with no shared denominator, the construction avoids the mechanical linkage that made the cash-share plus velocity rank-sum uninterpretable, and the hard screen should tighten the extreme deciles that currently generate conflicting FMB and alpha evidence.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( sale, sub( act, che ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: TurnoverLevelAndImprovementValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(sale, SUB(act, che)), 1), WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(sale, SUB(act, che)), 1), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness is most credible when accrual assets are both structurally fast-turning and currently accelerating: the level tells us the firm has a short cash cycle, the change tells us the cycle is not silently lengthening, and a cheap firm satisfying both is converting reported claims into realized revenue.
input_signals.reasoning: The two legs are the archive's only constructions strong on FMB, alpha, and Sharpe simultaneously, and unlike the rejected cash-share plus turnover pairing they are not mechanically linked through a shared denominator — one is a cross-sectional level, the other its own first difference. Winsorizing before ranking repairs the outlier defect the critic identified in both parents, so this is the natural consolidation test of the velocity channel.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( winsor( ratio( sale, sub( act, che ) ), 1 ), winsor( delta( ratio( sale, sub( act, che ) ), 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ProfitVelocityValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(act, che)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is not how much revenue passes through accrual assets but how much cash profit they generate: a cheap firm earning high operating profit per dollar of receivables and inventory has working capital that is genuinely productive, whereas high revenue throughput at zero margin means the accrual assets are being churned without creating value.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates whether the velocity channel works through throughput (sales) or through profit conversion (EBITDA) on the identical accrual-asset base, which distinguishes a DuPont-style turnover effect from a genuine cash-generation effect and tells us which quantity to build on in the final generations. It keeps the value weight and winsorization design that has produced joint evidence, changing only the numerator of the quality leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( ebitda, sub( act, che ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: VelocityAndDepreciationQualityValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(sale, SUB(act, che)), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(dp, MA(at, 3)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accounting quality has two independent dimensions for a cheap firm — how quickly its short-term accrual assets convert into revenue, and how conservatively it writes down its long-lived assets — and cheapness supported on both dimensions is least likely to be a value trap.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the mechanically correlated pairing the critic rejected: the two legs live in different regions of the balance sheet, so a firm with low operating working capital gains no automatic advantage on the depreciation leg. Both parents also had correctly signed FMB slopes (velocity 3.91, depreciation conservatism 2.86), so unlike the reversal-completion leg with its −1.68 slope, the composite has a coherent chance of joint cross-sectional and portfolio strength.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( winsor( ratio( sale, sub( act, che ) ), 1 ), winsor( ratio( dp, ma( at, 3 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: BuybackVerifiedCheapness
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cash returned by retiring shares is the hardest possible verification that a cheap firm's reported profits were actually collected, and it is credible only if the operating cycle was not simultaneously absorbing cash; a cheap firm shrinking its share count while releasing working capital is distributing real cash, whereas one issuing shares while building receivables and inventories is funding uncollected profit with equity.
input_signals.reasoning: This implements the payout-verification hypothesis with a continuously distributed financing variable rather than dividends, eliminating both the zero-payer mass point and the scale domination that made the previous expression collapse into the working-capital accrual leg. Combining the two legs in rank space guarantees each contributes equally by construction, so the signal genuinely tests financing-side cash return jointly with operating-side cash release.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( neg( growth( csho, 1 ) ), neg( winsor( ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: VelocityAndBuybackValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(sale, SUB(act, che)), 1), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The two strongest independent confirmations that a cheap firm's earnings are real are that it is retiring shares with cash and that its accrual assets are converting into revenue faster than before; a firm doing both is returning cash it has actually collected.
input_signals.reasoning: This pairs the archive's best Sharpe leg (share retirement, from BuybackVerifiedCheapness) with its best FMB leg (turnover improvement, fmb 3.62 with Sharpe 0.339), two channels drawn from different financial statements with no shared denominator, so the complementarity claim is clean unlike the earlier rejected pairings. If it beats both parents on ls_talpha and Sharpe, the final generations should build on financing-plus-velocity rather than financing-plus-accrual-level.

input_signals.name: TripleVerifiedCheapness
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(sale, SUB(act, che)), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1))))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness backed by three independent accounting confirmations — cash returned through share retirement, a structurally fast operating cycle, and working capital that is being released rather than absorbed — is the least likely to be a value trap, and the confirmations should aggregate rather than substitute.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the full consolidation of the three legs that have each produced correctly signed evidence, aggregated in bounded rank space so no leg dominates by scale. Its comparison against Signals 1 and 2 tells us whether accounting verification is genuinely multi-dimensional or whether one channel (financing discipline) subsumes the operating channels, which is the central question to answer before the final generations.

input_signals.name: HardBookAnchoredVerifiedValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ceq, SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc))), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The conditioning variable should itself be accrual-purged: measuring cheapness against book equity net of soft operating working capital ranks firms by hard-asset value per dollar of price, so the cash-verification legs are applied to a cleaner definition of who is genuinely cheap.
input_signals.reasoning: Every strong signal in the archive has used raw book-to-market as its weight, and HardBookToMarket was independently correctly signed (fmb 2.29), so upgrading the anchor while holding the winning quality composite fixed isolates the value-side design choice that has never been tested inside the successful architecture. If the alpha and Sharpe improve, the final signal should carry a purged anchor.

input_signals.name: DeleveragingVerifiedValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: If the buyback result reflects genuine cash generation rather than an equity-issuance anomaly, then debt repayment should work the same way: a cheap firm paying down borrowings while releasing working capital is servicing claims with collected cash, whereas one borrowing to fund receivables and inventories is financing uncollected profit.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the decisive economic test of what drives the archive's leading signal — cash verification, as hypothesized, or the published net-share-issuance effect — because it swaps the financing instrument while holding the operating leg and structure identical. A comparable result would establish the general mechanism; a null would tell the final generations that the equity-retirement channel is doing the work and should be kept explicit.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( neg( growth( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ) ), neg( winsor( ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: OwnHistoryCheapnessVerifiedValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What makes a value trap is not being cheap relative to other firms but being cheap relative to what this business has historically been worth; a firm trading at the top of its own five-year book-to-market range while retiring shares and releasing working capital is being discounted despite verified cash generation, and that discount should revert.
input_signals.reasoning: This changes the valuation side from a cross-sectional to a within-firm benchmark, a concept the archive has never tested on the value leg, and it does so for a specific portfolio reason: every cross-sectionally value-weighted construction here carries an HML/CMA loading that FF5 prices away, whereas an own-history cheapness weight is close to value-factor neutral and can only earn alpha through the verification channel. It keeps the winning verification composite intact so the comparison against BuybackVerifiedCheapness isolates the anchor concept rather than a parameter.

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single valuation ratio is a noisy measure of cheapness — book equity is distorted by write-offs and intangibles, revenue by margin structure — so a firm that is cheap on both an asset anchor and a revenue anchor is more reliably underpriced, and applying cash verification to that better-measured cheapness should sharpen the interaction.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the discredited third MIN-screen experiment with a measurement-error fix on the conditioning variable: agreement between two economically independent value anchors reduces the chance that the weight is picking up accounting distortion rather than genuine cheapness. It is complementary to, not overlapping with, HardBookAnchoredVerifiedValue, which purges the single anchor rather than diversifying across anchors, so the two together identify whether the value leg should be cleaned or broadened.

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), SUB(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), MA(at, 3)), RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(at, 3))))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cash verification of cheapness has a balance-sheet signature and a financing signature: the balance-sheet signature is that expansion shows up as cash rather than as receivables and inventories, and the financing signature is that shares are being retired; a cheap firm exhibiting both has collected its reported profits and is returning them.
input_signals.reasoning: The operating leg here is the full cash-versus-soft-capital composition that produced an independent positive alpha (+2.0%, t=2.17), which is strictly more informative than the working-capital-release half used by the current leader because it also credits firms that convert profits into cash balances. Both legs remain in bounded rank space and neither depends on velocity, so the test isolates whether adding the cash-accumulation side strengthens the archive's best signal.

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Buybacks and dividends are substitutable forms of the same evidence — cash actually leaving the firm — so total shareholder distribution is a stronger verification of a cheap firm's earnings than share retirement alone, provided the operating cycle is not simultaneously consuming that cash.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has never tested dividends inside a working construction; the earlier attempt failed because dvc was placed in a linear ratio where it was dominated by the working-capital term, whereas here it enters through its own rank so scale differences are irrelevant and the zero-payer mass merely occupies the bottom of one of three channels. If total payout beats buyback alone, the mechanism is cash distribution generally rather than the published net-issuance effect.

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The interaction can be read in either direction — a value premium that exists only among firms with verified accounting, or a quality premium that exists only among cheap firms — and the correct reading determines which variable should be the signed discriminator and which the bounded gate.
input_signals.reasoning: Every strong signal in the archive gates on value and lets accounting quality do the signing, which makes the spread nearly value-neutral and is plausibly why FF5 does not absorb it; this proposal reverses the roles so the extremes are high- and low-B/M firms drawn from the well-verified population. Comparing the two tells us whether the alpha comes from ranking value stocks by verification or from ranking verified stocks by value — an economically substantive question the archive cannot currently answer.

input_signals.name: SelfFundedGrowthValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), SUMRANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(sale, 1), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1))))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The strongest refutation of the value-trap interpretation is a cheap firm that is growing revenue while simultaneously releasing working capital and retiring shares — growth funded internally out of collected cash rather than out of accrual buildup or external issuance.
input_signals.reasoning: Revenue growth has never entered the archive as a channel, and it is the economically necessary complement to the working-capital leg: releasing working capital while the business shrinks is liquidation, whereas releasing it while revenue expands is genuine operating efficiency, so the two legs jointly identify a state that neither identifies alone. All three legs enter through ranks, so the growth term cannot dominate by scale and the conjunction is monotone in each channel.

input_signals.name: LongTermAccrualVerifiedValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(at, act), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Earnings can be inflated by capitalizing costs into long-lived assets just as easily as by building receivables, so a cheap firm whose non-current operating asset base is expanding faster than its revenue is deferring expenses onto the balance sheet, while one holding non-current assets flat relative to sales while retiring shares has earnings that are genuinely collected.
input_signals.reasoning: Every accrual leg tested so far has been confined to the working-capital cycle, yet the long-term operating accrual is the larger component of total accruals for capital-intensive firms and carries its own documented mispricing, so this extends the mechanism to a new region of the balance sheet rather than recombining tested elements. Deflating by three-year average sales keeps the interpretation as capitalization intensity relative to business volume, and coverage is as broad as the leading signals since it needs only total and current assets.

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), 0), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Whether working capital was released is more reliable evidence than how much was released, because magnitudes are dominated by one-off inventory writedowns and acquisitions; counting how many of the last three years showed a release identifies firms with a habitual discipline of collecting before they report.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the magnitude of the operating leg with a persistence count, a genuinely different statistic that is immune to the outliers that force winsorization and that measures a behavioural state rather than a single-year flow. Because the count takes only four values it also introduces deliberate coarseness, which should reduce portfolio turnover and, if the effect is real, raise the Sharpe of the spread relative to the magnitude-based parents.

input_signals.hypothesis: The specific state that destroys a value thesis is accrual buildup alongside falling revenue, so the correct quality discriminator is the *absence* of that conjunction, combined with evidence of cash being returned through share retirement.
input_signals.reasoning: The gen-7 trap signal delivered the right portfolio evidence (alpha −2.2%, t = −2.61) but a wrong-signed FMB slope, because multiplying a conjunctive red flag by the cheapness rank leaves the signal positively correlated with cheapness itself; embedding the negated red flag as one leg of the standard verification composite restores sign coherence between the two evaluation dimensions. It also converts a short-only diagnostic into a long-short signal built in the architecture that has repeatedly produced joint evidence.

input_signals.name: QualityMarkedBookToMarket
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(ceq, MUL(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(sale, SUB(act, che)))))), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
input_signals.hypothesis: Soft operating capital should be marked down in proportion to how slowly it turns rather than either counted at full book value or eliminated entirely: receivables and inventories that cycle rapidly are nearly cash, while those that sit are close to worthless, so the correct value anchor writes working capital down by its own illiquidity percentile.
input_signals.reasoning: This puts the accrual information inside the valuation ratio as a continuous haircut, which is a different construction from both raw book-to-market and the archive's HardBookToMarket that subtracts the entire working-capital balance regardless of its quality. It is also the first proposal here in which the interaction is intrinsic to the measurement of value rather than implemented as a gate times a quality score, so it tests whether the effect survives outside the winning architecture.

input_signals.name: ConservativeEarningsYield
input_signals.expression: RATIO(MIN(ib, SUB(ib, SUB(DELTA(wcap, 1), dp))), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
input_signals.hypothesis: A prudent investor prices a firm on the lower of its reported and its cash earnings, so positive accruals should be penalized while negative accruals earn no credit; the resulting asymmetric earnings yield identifies cheapness that holds up under the more conservative of two accounting measurements.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not the cash-flow-to-price ratio the critic rejected earlier, because MIN makes the accrual adjustment one-sided: firms whose cash flow exceeds income are valued on income, while firms whose income exceeds cash flow are valued on cash, so the numerator is a conservatism floor rather than a linear combination. The asymmetry is the economic content — accrual overstatement is punished, accrual understatement is not rewarded — and it can be tested only through a construction the archive has never used.

input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( min( ib, sub( ib, sub( delta( wcap, 1 ), dp ) ) ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) )

input_signals.name: LiquidationAnchoredVerifiedValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, lct), dltt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(sale, 3)), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Net-current-asset value per dollar of price is a liquidation-based claim on cheapness, and it is only meaningful if those current assets are actually realizable — so the accrual-verification requirement is far more binding for a liquidation anchor than for a going-concern book anchor, where earning power rather than asset realizability drives the discount.
input_signals.reasoning: Unlike the rejected multi-anchor proposal, this is not motivated by measurement error in cheapness but by a different economic claim: the liquidation anchor is built from the very current-asset accounts whose quality the verification leg tests, so the interaction is intrinsic rather than incidental and should be strictly stronger here than under book-to-market. Subtracting long-term debt keeps the anchor a genuine residual claim, and all inputs have coverage comparable to the leading signals.

input_signals.hypothesis: Share retirement, working-capital release, and revenue growth are three co-equal signatures of internally financed, cash-collected operations, and the value premium among cheap firms should be graded by how many of these signatures are present rather than dominated by any one of them.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs a concrete defect the critic identified in the archive's multi-leg composites: nested SUMRANK silently gives the outer leg twice the weight of each inner leg, so every three-channel signal tested so far has been a disguised two-thirds bet on share issuance. Summing three separately computed industry ranks enforces genuinely equal weighting, which is a structural correction with a testable prediction — if the equal-weighted version beats SelfFundedGrowthValue, the archive's earlier three-leg results understated the operating channels.

input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that NEG(MIN(a,b)) is a permissive "either flag absent" screen that discards much of the conjunctive information, so this replaces it with the strict product while holding the gate, the financing leg, the deflators and the aggregation identical. input_signals.hypothesis: What verifies a cheap firm's accounting is habit rather than magnitude on both sides of the ledger: how many of the last three years it retired shares, and how many it released working capital, with magnitudes discarded because they are dominated by one-off tenders, acquisitions and writedowns.

input_signals.name: ChronicTrapVerifiedValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)), NEG(TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), 0), INDICATOR(NEG(GROWTH(sale, 1)), 0)), 3)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year of accrual buildup during a demand decline can be a cyclical accident, but a firm that has been in that state repeatedly over three years is chronically failing to convert reported sales into cash; the count of trap-years, not its current severity, is what separates a temporarily depressed cheap stock from a deteriorating one.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not a recombination of the two frontier legs but a new statistic applied to the trap state itself — chronicity rather than either current intensity (TrapFreeVerifiedValue) or the frequency of the benign state (PersistentReleaseVerifiedValue) — so a positive result identifies persistence of the *pathology* as the operative concept and a null cleanly rules it out. Because the count is discrete and slow-moving, it should produce a stable low-turnover portfolio while the retirement leg supplies the continuous cash-return dimension.

input_signals.hypothesis: What protects a cheap firm is the ability to turn accrual assets back into cash when needed: if over five years its largest working-capital release exceeds its largest buildup, the operating cycle is flexible and the receivables and inventories on its balance sheet are genuinely realizable, whereas a firm that builds sharply and never releases holds claims it cannot monetize.
input_signals.reasoning: Summing the five-year maximum and minimum of the working-capital flow measures the *asymmetry* of the accrual distribution — a third-moment concept that the archive has never tested, distinct from the level, change, persistence count, and volatility formulations, and economically distinct because it speaks to realizability under stress rather than to average discipline. It also replaces the failed volatility experiment with the right sign logic: instability per se was not informative, but release-skewed instability should be, and unlike the earlier attempt the flow is sales-deflated and winsorized so cash-heavy firms cannot drive the extremes.
